title: Dedicated: Performance Profiles (Hardware Tuning) — Customer Messaging Draft
body:
Audience: Dedicated customers (technical evaluators + platform owners), plus CS/CSEs and Sales Engineering using this as a talk track.

Status: draft. Please leave comments inline + call out any statements that over-promise SLOs.

---

1) What are “Performance Profiles” (and why we’re introducing them)

Redwood’s runtime has a set of tuning knobs that affect how we serve LLM requests on GPUs: kernel variants, batching/scheduling behavior, KV cache/memory allocator settings, and safety guardrails.

A “Performance Profile” is a versioned bundle of these tuned settings, validated for a specific GPU type and a set of common workload shapes (prompt/response length + concurrency patterns).

Why this matters:
- More consistent performance across time and across regions for the same hardware SKU (e.g., Dedicated H100 in us-east vs eu-west).
- Faster, safer improvements: we can ship performance fixes as profile versions with clear change notes and rollback.
- Better observability: Redwood can tell you exactly which profile is active when you’re debugging latency, throughput, or OOM behavior.

What this is NOT:
- A model change. Profiles tune serving behavior; they don’t change your prompts or your model weights.
- A “set it and forget it” promise that no performance characteristics will ever change. Profiles help us manage changes explicitly and safely.

Supported hardware (initial):
- H100 (production)
- L40S (production)
- B200 (early / preview; requires explicit enablement)

---

2) What improves for Dedicated customers

We want customers to feel two things:
(1) performance becomes more predictable, and
(2) changes become easier to control.

Expected improvements (general):
- More stable tail latency under mixed workloads (short prompts + long prompts happening together).
- Fewer “surprise regressions” from runtime upgrades because we gate, canary, and document profile changes.
- Better protection against overload/OOM by using SKU-specific headroom and admission control.
- Clearer root-cause signals: queueing vs compute, kernel fallback rates, KV cache pressure.

How to quantify it (how we’ll talk about it):
- We can share benchmark methodology and directional results (e.g., lower p99 variance; better sustained tokens/sec at a given concurrency) rather than promising a fixed % improvement for every workload.
- For Dedicated renewals and expansions: we can commit to change-management controls (pin/rollback) and improved transparency (active profile + version surfaced).

Suggested phrasing (customer-friendly):
“Think of profiles as Redwood’s ‘best known configuration’ for your GPU type. They are tested, versioned, and observable. You can stay on Redwood-managed defaults, or pin a known-good version if you want maximum stability.”

---

3) What might change (and what customers should watch)

We should be upfront: some tuning changes trade throughput vs latency, and some improve stability by being more conservative.

Things that can change across profile versions:
- Throughput at high concurrency (tokens/sec) due to different batching behavior.
- Tail latency (p95/p99) depending on workload mixture and queue policy.
- Max safe concurrency / request admission thresholds (often tightened to protect tail latency or prevent OOM).
- Memory headroom and KV cache behavior (which may reduce peak throughput to avoid fragmentation/OOM).
- Kernel selection/fallback behavior (usually invisible, but can impact long-context or specific model families).

Things that should NOT change:
- API contract and request/response formats.
- Your model choice and model version pin (if you’ve pinned one).
- Data isolation for Dedicated.

Recommended customer metrics to watch after any upgrade or profile change:
- Request latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) by route/model
- Error rate (timeouts, 429/overload, 5xx)
- Queueing time vs compute time (if exposed in your dashboards / our console view)
- GPU memory usage and OOM events

Messaging note:
We should not lead with “kernels” and “allocator settings.” Lead with “consistency, safer upgrades, and control.” Then provide technical detail if asked.

---

4) Control: pinning, change windows, and rollback

Key customer concern: “If something changes, can I freeze it / revert quickly?”

Pinning (customer-controlled stability)
- Dedicated customers can request to pin a specific performance profile version for their cluster/pool.
- Pinning keeps the profile stable across runtime patch upgrades unless explicitly changed.
- We will only allow pins to versions that are compatible with your hardware/driver baseline and meet safety guardrails.

Roll forward (adopting newer profiles)
- Redwood will publish release notes describing profile changes (what changed, why, and what to monitor).
- For Dedicated: we will treat profile changes as opt-in by default (TBD — see open question), or coordinate on a change window for managed upgrades.

Rollback (if regression observed)
- If a profile update results in a material regression for your workload, we can roll back to the previous pinned version.
- Rollback is designed to be fast and low-risk (configuration change + restart/reload depending on deployment topology).
- Support/SRE will have an audit trail of changes (who changed what, when) to speed incident response.

Suggested customer-facing guarantee language (careful):
“We support pin/rollback of performance profile versions on Dedicated. If you see an unexpected regression after a change, we can revert quickly while we investigate.”

---

5) Proposed customer comms format

A) Short announcement email (for existing Dedicated customers)

Subject: Introducing versioned Performance Profiles for more predictable Dedicated inference

Hi <Name>,

We’re rolling out versioned Performance Profiles for Redwood Dedicated. Profiles are Redwood-validated runtime configurations tuned per GPU type (e.g., H100, L40S) to improve consistency and make performance changes easier to control.

What you’ll get:
- More predictable latency/throughput behavior on your hardware
- Better tail-latency stability under mixed request patterns
- Explicit versioning with the option to pin a known-good profile and roll back if needed

What might change:
- Some profile updates may adjust batching/concurrency behavior to improve stability; this can shift throughput vs latency depending on workload.

If you’d like, we can (1) share the benchmark methodology, and (2) set a change window to adopt the latest profile—or pin your current profile version for maximum stability.

Best,
<CSM/SE Name>

B) Release note snippet (for upgrade notes)
- Added: runtime reports active profile ID + version in debug/health.
- Default profile updates per SKU (H100/L40S) with “what to watch” bullets.
- Rollback instructions and who to contact.

C) FAQ block for CSMs/SEs

Q: Are you changing the model?
A: No. Profiles tune serving behavior. Your model pin (if any) remains unchanged.

Q: Will this change my SLO?
A: Your Dedicated SLO terms don’t change automatically. Profiles are designed to improve consistency; we’ll coordinate any meaningful changes and can pin/rollback.

Q: Can I stay on my current behavior?
A: Yes. We can pin your profile version so it doesn’t change unexpectedly.

Q: How do I know what profile I’m on?
A: Redwood will surface the active profile (ID + version) in operational views (Console/debug bundle). Support can also confirm.

Q: What if I have a very unusual workload shape?
A: Profiles cover common workload buckets; if you’re an outlier we’ll use pinning and targeted tuning/guardrails. The goal is controlled overrides, not one-off mystery configs.

---

6) Internal guidance: what NOT to say

Avoid:
- “This will make everything faster.” (Not true across all workloads.)
- “No more regressions.” (We reduce risk; we don’t eliminate it.)
- Deep kernel or driver specifics unless the customer is explicitly asking (and even then keep it high level).

Do say:
- “Versioned, tested, observable.”
- “Safer upgrades, with pin/rollback.”
- “Tuned per GPU SKU and workload shape.”

---

7) Open questions / TODOs

TODO (Product + SRE): Decide and document Dedicated default posture
- Option A: Dedicated is opt-in for profile updates by default.
- Option B: Redwood-managed default updates with an agreed change window and clear rollback.
- Strong preference from customer conversations: opt-in or at least a clear “no surprises” policy for larger Dedicated accounts.

TODO (Docs): What will customers see in Console vs via Support?
- Minimal: profile_version string and SKU.
- Possibly: high-level “performance characteristics” table (e.g., recommended max concurrency bands) without exposing sensitive internals.

TODO (Sales/CS enablement): One-page internal enablement
- Talk track + when to recommend pinning (e.g., during a POC, before a big launch, or after a regression incident).

TODO (Legal/Contracts): Confirm whether “pin/rollback” needs to be included in Dedicated order forms or is best-effort.

---

8) Notes from recent customer signals (for context; not customer-facing)
- SUP-21941: customer perceived higher p99 after upgrade; fastest mitigation was pinning and quickly rolling back one batching default.
- SUP-22007: repeated request during POC: “Can we pin the serving behavior while we validate?” This messaging should make pinning feel normal and supported.

Owner: Lauren
Next review: align with Mateo/Sean on exact rollback semantics + what’s guaranteed vs best-effort. Then send to Elliot/Kira for external-facing tone check.
